everyone sees that he has brought upon himself the hatred of many.
Those who are of very sharp judgment in weighing the speech of men: let them see this argument, read it, and carefully investigate whether anything offends, and if something does not please them, let them not immediately knit their brows or curl their lips. Let them place their faith in the judgment of the more learned, who will bring forth none but a true judgment concerning my <term>Carolus</term> <gloss>Charles</gloss>. For who, I ask, does not see how brilliantly he handles this most difficult argument? The weight of almost every single word is matched by the words themselves, which is rare among theologians, and the material is not disproportionate to the thoughts. And to sum up my differences, they are seen to be so apt that he seems to excel not only modern writers, but even <term>Hieronymus</term> <gloss>Jerome</gloss> himself, if I dare say so. For although he is frugal with words above all else, he is nevertheless rich in thoughts; he is not barren, nor does he wither away in sterility. If you seek medicinal sweetness and delight, no one, in truth, soothes the ears more fully, penetrates minds more vividly, or urges more intensely. To these ends, therefore, most holy pastor, I have labored more diligently so that the excellence of your magnificence might be more nobly exalted, and I have sent this argument, which it does not shame any prelate to know, to your own <term>Celsitudo</term> <gloss>Highness</gloss>. I have imitated certain ones, whose names have escaped me through negligence, who never greet their King without a gift. It was my intention to suppress the praises of your virtues and rare good fortune, lest I appear a vain flatterer, for I know that you are no more moved by praises than a bleary-eyed man is by painted tablets. Although you are considered a favorite of both birth and fortune, I pass over other bodily gifts. Nevertheless, that which is taken from <term>Cato Uticensis</term> <gloss>Cato the Younger</gloss> can be truthfully and ingenuously said of you: You are the true image of virtue.

Therefore, most holy shepherd, in order that the excellence of your magnificence might be more nobly exalted, I have labored zealously to send this subject—which it does not disgrace any prelate to know—to your own <term>Celsitudo</term> <gloss>Highness/Excellence</gloss>. I have imitated certain men, whose names have slipped my mind through negligence, who never greet their King without a gift. It was my intention to suppress the praise of your virtues and rare good fortune, lest I appear a vain flatterer. I know that you are no more moved by praises than a bleary-eyed man is by paintings. Although you may be considered a product of either birth or fortune—I say nothing of your other physical gifts—what was said of that Cato of Utica <note>original: "Cato Uticensis"</note> can still be honestly said of you: You are the true image of virtue <note>original: "virtutis ymago"</note>.

if fiery meteors were to be formed in this way, it would be necessary for another fiery meteor to arise from the smoke of a falling star, and from the smoke of this one another, and so on to infinity, which nature abhors. Furthermore, an effect is never more noble than its cause. Nor is the author consistent here, as he says that windy meteors arise from vapor and smoke. Yet these are more correctly and better said to be produced by air, or by the spirit enclosed within the earth, which originates from air. For the qualities of vapor and smoke do not have the same affinity with the qualities of windy meteors as air does. And he seems to have erred in this, when he asserts that springs arise from airy atoms enclosed and condensed within the earth, which we deny entirely. For as to the first point, namely that springs are made from atoms, his opinion is absurd, since one would have to count how many atoms would be required for a whole spring, when even a single tiny drop consists of many myriads of atoms. Indeed, his statement that springs are formed from condensed airy atoms conflicts with the opinion of the physicists, who hold that the elements are not transmuted such that water is made from air. Moreover, the effect is such as its cause: the effect is water, therefore it is necessary that the cause is also water. And although a certain spring may sometimes appear to arise anew, it does not so much arise anew as it is made manifest from being hidden. But more may be said of this at another time.

§ 15. It remains for us to offer a few words on corruption, through which these smallest bodies, once formed, each tend toward their own species. When all bodies rot, they emit much vapor or smoke, which are nothing other than contiguous bodies composed of many myriads of atoms, which do not pass into nothingness, but are separated under an invisible form, and each returns to its own species. We provide the example of fire for this: if you sprinkle water on a frost, the fire vanishes; it would be wrong to say that there is an annihilation of the fire here, and that it dies, but rather it is hidden by its enemy, which denies it the necessary ventilation. Consider further the combustion of a certain body, in which the conversion of the body into fire does not occur, but rather its resolution into its smallest parts, which, when gathered, are dissipated and dissolved so that they can no longer be seen, although when joined they could be seen. If one asks where these smallest parts go after corruption occurs, we answer: into the vacuum, so that they may replenish it. For there is no vacuum in nature, because nature is a lover of unity. There are still other things that these smallest parts of nature accomplish, which are worthy of dissertation.

<summary>The author critiques a theory of elemental transformation, arguing against the idea that springs and meteors arise from the transmutation of airy atoms, and further explains the process of corruption as the resolution of bodies into invisible parts rather than their annihilation.</summary>
<keywords>atoms, meteors, springs, corruption, elements, vacuum, physics, transmutation</keywords>

Moreover, an effect is never nobler than its cause. The author is also not consistent in claiming that windy meteors arise from vapor and smoke. It is better and more accurate to say that these phenomena are produced by air, or by the spirit enclosed within the earth that originates from the air. The qualities of vapor and smoke do not have the same affinity with the qualities of windy meteors as the air does. He also seems to have erred in stating that springs arise from airy atoms enclosed and condensed within the earth, a claim we entirely reject. For the first point, the idea that springs are made of atoms is absurd; how many atoms would be required for a whole spring, when even a single drop consists of many myriads of atoms? Furthermore, his claim that springs are formed from condensed airy atoms contradicts the opinion of physicists who maintain that elements are not transmuted, such that water is made from air. Moreover, the cause must match the effect; the effect is water, therefore the cause must also be water. And although a certain spring may sometimes seem to arise anew, it is not so much born anew as it is revealed after having been hidden. More could be said about this at another time.

§ 15. It remains for us to offer a few words regarding corruption, by which these minimal bodies <note>referring to atoms</note> tend toward their own species when the composed body is destroyed. All bodies, when they decay, emit much vapor or smoke, which are nothing other than contiguous bodies composed of many myriads of atoms. These do not vanish into nothingness but are separated in an invisible form, and each returns to its own kind. We provide the example of fire: if you sprinkle water on a flame, the fire vanishes. It is incorrect to say that this is an annihilation of fire or that it perishes; it is merely hidden by an enemy <note>water</note> that denies it the ventilation it requires. Consider further the combustion of a body, in which there is no conversion of the body into fire, but a resolution into its minimal parts, which, when gathered together, are dissipated and dissolved so that they can no longer be seen, even though they were visible when combined. If it is asked where these minimal parts go when corruption occurs, we answer: into a vacuum, so that they may fill it. For a vacuum is not found in nature, because nature loves unity. There are other things that these minimal particles of nature perform which would be worthy of discussion.

<summary>The author critiques the theories of others regarding the formation of meteors and springs from atomic resolution, arguing instead for the stability of elements, and explains that corruption is a process of separation rather than annihilation, with atoms filling the vacuum of nature.</summary>

**CESSION)** This differs from the process of concurrence. If someone wishes to make a cession of goods, there is a need for the harassment of creditors, which is not the case in a concurrence. A cession of goods can be made regarding certain creditors, whereas a concurrence involves all of them. Hence, in a cession, an edictal citation is not strictly necessary; see Salgado, <note>part 1, chapter 1, number 46 and following</note>. However, when a concurrence has been initiated, a cession of goods must always follow (concerning which our Author writes here), but not vice versa.

**CURATOR)** This applies if it has been so determined by the creditors, at whose risk the matter is handled. Indeed, the administration is sometimes entrusted to the widow of the deceased, so that she may render accounts to the creditors; but this is dangerous, since the debtor and his widow are equally concerned more with their own advantage than with that of the creditors, so that it is more advisable to appoint another curator. 33. From this, one may conclude that not all Stoics approved of suicide <note>original: "propricidium"</note> without distinction. Furthermore, even if this were granted, it does not follow that all legal experts <term>Jurisconsulti</term> <gloss>Roman legal scholars/jurists</gloss> were Stoics. And if this were also conceded, it still does not follow that they approved of self-killing <term>αυτοχειριαν</term> <gloss>suicide</gloss>. By that same reasoning, we could conclude that all other Stoic dogmas were accepted by the legal experts, for example, that all sins are equal, or that a wise man does not lie, and so on. There is also no logical consequence that because some legal experts were Stoics and approved of self-killing, therefore it is permitted under civil law. This would only follow if our law were to be judged by the initial composition of the legal experts, and not by the authority of the Emperor Justinian, who was a Christian and instructed in the Holy Scriptures. Regarding the cited laws, in addition to the answer provided by Heigius, it can be said that the texts speak only of the confiscation of property. One who commits self-killing is not subject to this unless they have laid violent hands upon themselves out of fear of punishment. Yet, it does not follow from this that self-killing is lawful by right or entirely unpunished. Indeed, this consequence is invalidated by Law 2 in the Code, where the fiscal cause—the confiscation of property—is contrasted with the death penalty, and self-killing is termed a crime.

# CHAPTER II.

A person is punished with death for a crime by someone established in a public office. This is required by divine justice, the safety of the republic, and for the sake of the delinquents themselves. For God does not wish to acquit the wicked, nor in any way justify the guilty, but His justice requires that it go well with the good and ill with the evil. Thus, David says in Psalm 101, "In the morning I will destroy all the wicked of the land, that I may cut off all evildoers from the city of God." The safety of the republic demands it. It is testified in Novella 77, chapter 1, at the beginning, that entire cities have perished on account of crimes. And if crimes are left unpunished, peace and tranquility are driven away. In order for these to be preserved, the magistrate must act diligently so that the republic is rid of evil men, and so that the sacrilegious, robbers, kidnappers, and thieves are punished in the due manner, as taught by Ulpian in Law 13 of the Digest concerning the duty of a governor. For to these men they must show themselves terrible, so that the punishment of a few may gradually render all others safe. The cause of the delinquents themselves likewise desires this. For punishments are established for their own reformation, as stated in Law 20 on punishments, and so that those who have sown iniquity may reap trouble, according to Proverbs 22, verse 8.

XXXIIII.
Hence, he who had dealt and transacted with his guardians solely regarding the agreement of his administered guardianship, when acting against the same guardians in the person of his brother, to whom he had become heir, is not precluded by the prescription of the transaction that was made.

XXXV.
Hence also, a transaction made concerning a will does not extend to codicils found afterward.

XXXVI.
Regarding Law 2 of the Code on rescinding sales <note>original: "l. 2. C. de rescind. vend."; referring to the Codex Justinianus on the rescission of sales due to lesion</note>, whether it has a place in a transaction, the opinions of interpreters are contradictory. Having rejected the affirmative view of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a prominent 14th-century jurist</note>, I shall defend the negative view of Jason <note>Jason de Mayno, a prominent 15th-century jurist</note>: a point which the Imperial Chamber <note>the *Reichskammergericht*, the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> has confirmed by its judgments, although I do not deny that the opposite is almost observed in certain other courts.

XXXVII.
A transaction imposes an end upon doubtful matters and uncertain lawsuits, and is held in place of the truth, just as a matter adjudged <term>res judicata</term> <gloss>a case already decided by a court</gloss>.

XXXVIII.
And this is so true that causes or lawsuits ended by legitimate transactions cannot be revived, not even by an imperial rescript.

XXXIX.

A person is punished with death for a crime by one who is established in public office. For this is required by divine justice, the safety of the republic, and for the sake of the delinquents themselves. It is testified in Novella 77, chapter 1, at the beginning, that entire cities have perished because of crimes. And if crimes are left unpunished, peace and quiet are expelled; however, in order that peace be preserved, the magistrate must act with diligence so that the Republic may be rid of evil men, and so that the sacrilegious, robbers, kidnappers, and thieves may be punished in the proper way, as Ulpian teaches in law 13 of the Digest, under the section on the duty of the governor. ## 1. The Origins of the Work

Our text has long been considered a somewhat belated countermeasure of Catholic controversial theology against the publication of Melanchthon’s *Loci communes* <gloss>Common Places</gloss>. As early as one year after the appearance of the *Enchiridion* <gloss>Handbook</gloss>, Zwingli wrote to Vadian: "Eck has explained certain common places, having imitated Melanchthon, as I suppose..."¹. However, if Melanchthon was the model, the practical initiative came—as Eck himself recounts—from the legate Lorenzo Campeggio⁵.

That, however, is not the whole story. Eck had been entertaining the idea of a comprehensive refutation, not limited to individual topics or specific works of Reformation theology, since as early as 1523. We can even trace the emergence of such a plan in his work with some precision.

It is well known that in 1520, Eck played a very active role in Rome in the drafting of the bull of excommunication *Exsurge Domine* <gloss>Arise, O Lord</gloss>, especially, it seems, in the selection of Lutheran writings that had not been considered in the *Condemnationes* <gloss>Condemnations</gloss> of Cologne and Louvain⁶. At the same time, he had begun to participate actively in that production of polemical writings which Hubert Jedin⁷ has described as the "flood tide of publicity."

Only a few of the writings published before 1523 deal with a large number of different controversial issues. In Fabri’s *Malleus* <gloss>Hammer</gloss>, for example, many of these are treated rather marginally, and the work concentrates largely on the questions of Church and authority that were at the forefront for the Roman Catholic interlocutor. **Page 1.** Giovanni Colonna was the second son of Stefano, the head of the house of Colonna at this time. Petrarch was on a footing of intimate friendship with several members of this family. There are sixteen letters addressed to Giovanni, as well as several metrical epistles and the sonnet, *Rime* cclxvi. In *Sen.* xvi. 1 Petrarch gives an account of his friendship with the younger brother Giacomo; while both were students at the University of Bologna they had been attracted to one another, but it was not until after Petrarch’s return to Avignon in April 1326 that they became friends. (F. Lo Parco has tried to show in *Errors in the Biography of Petrarch* <note>original: "Errori . . . nella biogr. del P."</note>, ‘Journal of Italian Literary History’ <note>original: "Giorn. stor. d. lett. ital."</note>, xlviii, 1906, pp. 37-69, that Petrarch returned to Avignon at the end of 1325, and as a result puts back by a year the date of a number of the earlier letters. But the case against the traditional date, 1326, is not proved. See also P. de Nolhac, *Petrarch at Bologna in the Time of Azzo Visconti* <note>original: "P. à Bologne au temps d’Azzo Visconti"</note>, in ‘Petrarch and Lombardy’ <note>original: "P. e la Lombardia"</note>, Milan, 1904, pp. 87-93.) Giacomo, now Bishop of Lombez, took Petrarch with him to his see in Gascony (on this journey see F. Lo Parco, *Petrarch and Giacomo Colonna at Toulouse* <note>original: "Il P. e Giacomo Colonna a Tolosa"</note>, in ‘Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Archaeology . . . in Naples’ <note>original: "Mem. d. R. Accad. di archeol. . . . in Napoli"</note>, 1911, pt. 2, p. 229 seq.), and on their return to Avignon in 1330 introduced him to his brother the Cardinal. From 1330-7 Petrarch was living in the Cardinal’s house at Avignon, and was probably to some extent dependent on him. It was not until 1335 that he received his first Church preferment, a canonry at Lombez. The Cardinal probably paid the expenses of the journey which this letter describes, and we shall hear of Petrarch’s securing his consent for his visit to Rome in 1337. Giovanni was created a Cardinal by Pope John XXII in 1327 before he had reached the age of thirty. For other details of Petrarch’s relations with the family see *Fam.* iv. 6, v. 3, and viii. 1.

# Cap. III.
## On the Jurisconsults of Roman Law.

<note>A decorative initial letter A begins the chapter.</note> Under the Emperor Augustus, there was already in Rome, as Livy speaks (book 3, ch. 34), an immense heap of laws piled one upon another, or, to use the words of Tacitus (Annals, book 3, ch. 25), as it had previously suffered from crimes, so then it suffered from laws, because by that time the multitude and variety of laws had reached an infinite state. Therefore, just as for some time the forums and courts of that city could not have functioned without industrious legal expertise, so too, from such a number and diversity of laws, the authority of men in that profession grew not a little by a kind of necessity, contrary to what had been customary there or elsewhere in the world until then. Furthermore, as to who professed the science of Roman Law before that age, one must look to Pomponius on the origin of law. In that age, Atejus Capito and Antistius Labeo were of the greatest authority. These two, to use the words of Pomponius, first created what were essentially different sects; for Capito persevered in those things which had been handed down to him, whereas Labeo, because of the quality of his intellect and confidence in his learning—having also devoted his efforts to other works of wisdom—began to innovate in many areas. Furthermore, it is established from Pomponius that both had disciples: Massurius Sabinus for Capito, and Nerva for Labeo, who increased these dissensions still further, namely in the age of Tiberius, Claudius, and Gaius. <margin>Some remarkable examples of how the ancients stole things from each other.</margin>

Thus, Justinus borrowed all his material from Trogus Pompeius, and Julius Solinus in a certain way copied Pliny. Thus, Lucian and Apuleius enriched themselves with Lucius of Patrae <note>original: "Lucio Pratense"</note>; both lived at the same time and both copied the same book and inserted it into their own famous books, and one calls his *Lucius*, the other calls his *The Golden Ass*. In the same way, Simocatta dealt with Diodorus Siculus in his book about the Nile, as one can see from the work appended to Herocletus and translated by Jungermann. Thus, Eratosthenes completely rewrote Timotheus on the Islands, so much so that he did not even make a different preface, but kept the previous one. Strabo recounts the same of Eudorus and Ariston in a book that also has the title *On the Nile*. Clement of Alexandria recorded many such examples among the Greeks, and Pliny speaks of this quite clearly in his preface, namely that when he held his authors against one another and read one work alongside the other, he found that generally the successors wrote their own material word for word from the ancients, yet never mentioned their books with a single word. Not to mention that the ingenious work of Ovid belongs more to Parthenius of Nicaea than to him, and the highly famous Virgil borrowed all his works from others: namely the Eclogues or shepherd dialogues from Theocritus; the Georgics, or on agriculture, from Hesiod and Aratus; the books on Aeneas from Homer, among which he took the second book, in which he tells the story of Sinon and the Trojan Horse (as Macrobius notes), word for word from Pisander. Our own art (of medicine) is also not free from this: as Oribasius, Aetius, and Aegineta wrote their own material in a certain way from Galen; but Marcellus Empiricus, who left behind a famous work on medicines, copied such things word for word from Scribonius Largus on the composition of medicines, and did not even leave out his concluding speech. From this we can see that the ancients were also only men, just like us. Likewise, Lucian and Apuleius enriched themselves with Lucius of Patrae; both lived at the same time and both copied the same book, setting it into their own famous works, with one calling his *Lucius* and the other his *The Golden Ass*. In the same way, Simocatta dealt with Diodorus Siculus in his book on the Nile. As one can see from the work appended to Heraclitus and translated by Jungermann. Thus, Eratosthenes entirely transcribed Timotheus of the Islands, so much so that he did not even write a different preface but kept the previous one. Strabo recounts similar instances regarding Eudorus and Ariston in a book that also bears the title *On the Nile*. Clement of Alexandria recorded many such examples among the Greeks; and Pliny speaks of this quite clearly in his preface, namely that when he held his writers up against one another and read through one work alongside another, he found that the successors generally copied their material word for word from the ancients, yet never mentioned their books with a single word. Not to mention that the ingenious work of Ovid belongs more to Parthenius of Nicaea than to him, and the highly famous Virgil borrowed all his works from others: namely, the Eclogues or shepherd dialogues from Theocritus; the Georgics, or on agriculture, from Hesiod and Aratus; and the books on Aeneas from Homer, from which he took the second book, in which he recounts the story of Sinon and the Trojan horse, (as Macrobius notes) word for word from Pisander. Even our own art (of medicine) is not free from this: just as Oribasius, Aetius, and Aegineta wrote their material in a certain way from Galen; but Marcellus Empiricus, who left behind a famous work on medicines, copied it word for word from Scribonius Largus's *On the Composition of Medicines*, and did not even leave out his concluding speech. Another comes and takes them, and the tree does not take them back. So also, what is it to your profit that you perform good works out of faith? It profits you nothing; another takes your works, and that is God. Humans take from the pear tree, for they possess the place of God on earth in temporal things; therefore, they are an earthly god. And just as little as the tree enjoys its fruit, just so little do you enjoy your works, even when they emerge at their best from faith. Thus, the praise belongs to the good pears, not the tree. In the pears, the tree is honored, not in the pears themselves. Therefore, note this further: Although the tree does not enjoy its fruit, it does not cease to bear it; it brings it forth every year, provided it is a good tree in its blossom, it bears them. Likewise, although works do not profit the believer, he does not abandon them, for it is the nature of faith that it is not without fruit, just as a good tree is not without pears. And in the same way, when autumn comes, as the pears fall from the tree and leave the tree standing alone, leave it to be covered in snow, frost, etc., and know it no longer; so, in the autumn of judgment over the sinner, all his works fall away from him, leave him standing alone, and leave him to answer for himself alone. And just as pears rot and decay, so your works fade and disappear, and leave you alone. But in the same way that the pears are taken from the tree and kept in a chest, so also will your works be preserved as a testimony that you were a good tree. But they will not place you higher or lower, just as little as the pears do the tree; another eats them. Thus it happens to your works also; another eats them, and not you.

Since he also says that "the living separate a specific place for the dying ants, and that there are ancestral monuments for them there," we must say that the more praises he heaps upon irrational animals, the more he—even against his will—enhances the work of the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Divine Reason/Word</gloss> that ordered all things. He demonstrates that the ingenuity in human beings is capable of embellishing, through the use of reason, even the advantages found in the nature of irrational creatures. And why do I say "irrational," since it seems to Celsus that those things commonly called irrational are not even irrational at all? Certainly, the man who professed to speak about the nature of the whole, and who boasted of the truth in the title of his book, does not think even ants are irrational. For he speaks about the ants conversing with one another in such terms as these: "And indeed, when they meet, they converse with one another, which is why they do not miss their paths. Therefore, there is also a completion of speech among them, and common notions of certain universal things, and voice, and objects that exist, and things signified." For to converse with another occurs through a voice that reveals something signified, and often it also reports about so-called existing objects. How would it not be the most ridiculous thing of all to say that these things exist in ants?

### III.

If any number of given magnitudes are added together, the magnitude composed of them will also be given.

For let any number of given magnitudes, *AB* and *BΓ*, be added together. I say that the magnitude *AΓ*, composed of *AB* and *BΓ*, is also given.

For since the magnitude *AB* is given, it is possible for a magnitude equal to it to be constructed <note>original: "comparetur"</note> [Def. 1]. Let it be constructed, and let it be *ΔE*. Again, since the magnitude *BΓ* is given, it is possible for a magnitude equal to it to be constructed [Def. 1]. Let it be constructed, and let it be *EZ*. Now, since *AB* = *ΔE* and *BΓ* = *EZ*, the whole *AΓ* will be equal to the whole *ΔZ* [Common Notion 2]. Therefore, the magnitude *AΓ* is given [Def. 1], for the magnitude *ΔZ* has been constructed equal to it.

**262. Sileni:** These are not Homeric, whether in the singular or plural. The related Satyrs occur first in Hesiod, *Fragment* 198 (44), where they are associated with the mountain-nymphs. The Sileni frequently appear as lovers of nymphs on vases; also on coins of Thasos. For Hermes and the nymphs, cf. *Homeric Hymn* xix. 34 (lover of Dryope), and often.

**264 f.** This passage is the first to mention the concept that the life of the tree-nymphs (Dryads, Adryads, Hamadryads) is bound up with the trees. The belief appears not uncommonly in poetry after Pindar. 

**264. The fir and oak are, of course,**

<column-break/>

only representatives of trees in general. The Dryad stands for any tree-nymph, although the name must go back to the very early time when special reverence was paid to the oak. Cf. Pausanias x. 32. 6: "They (the nymphs) grew from other trees and especially from the oaks."

**267, 268.** These verses have been suspected, partly on the ground of the asyndeton <note>the omission of conjunctions between words or clauses</note>. The asyndeton of **ἑστᾶσ’** <gloss>they stand</gloss> is excused by the opening of the parenthesis. The pronoun **ἑ** <gloss>them/her</gloss> has also been a cause of concern; it is unique as a plural, but cf. **ἑᾶς** <gloss>their own</gloss> of a plural subject in Pindar, *Pythian Odes* iv. 187, which seems to justify the use. It is possible that the writer has blindly copied such passages as *Odyssey* iv. 355: "Pharos, as they call it."

**ἠλίβατοι:** In Homer, this obscure word is found only in connection with rock, and is taken to mean "abrupt" or "precipitous." In *Odyssey* ix. 243 and Hesiod, *Theogony* 675, it is an epithet of a stone in the sense of a moveable rock, not a cliff. There is a further extension of the meaning in Hesiod, *Theogony* 483: a "deep" cave; and in *Shield of Heracles* 421, Rzach reads with one manuscript "as when an oak or pine, high and lofty, fell." We need not therefore suspect the use of the word when it is applied here to trees.

**262. Sileni:** Not Homeric, either in the singular or plural. The related <term>Satyroi</term> <gloss>Satyrs</gloss> occur first in Hesiod, fragment 198 (44), where they are associated with the mountain-nymphs. The Sileni frequently appear as lovers of nymphs on vases and on coins of Thasos. For Hermes and the nymphs, see hymn XIX. 34 and other instances.

**Keen-sighted <note>original: "εὔσκοπος"</note>:** For the trisyllabic form, see *h. Ap.* 36. Hermann omitted **te** (and) to conform to Homeric usage.

**264 f.** This passage is the first to contain a definitive mention of the idea that the life of the tree-nymphs (dryads, adryads, hamadryads) is bound up with their trees. This belief appears often in poetry after Pindar. Examples include Pindar's fragment 146, the scholia on Apollonius, and Callimachus’ *Hymn to Delos* 83 f., which asks if oaks truly were born when the nymphs were born, noting that nymphs rejoice when rain feeds the oaks and mourn when the trees lose their leaves. Apollonius of Rhodes, Nonnus, and Ovid also record this connection. Similarly, the life of tree spirits in Czech and German folklore, such as the <term>Moosleute</term> <gloss>moss-folk</gloss> and <term>Elfen</term> <gloss>elves</gloss>, depends on the tree.

**264. The fir and oak are, of course,**

<column-break/>

only representatives of trees in general. The Dryad stands for any tree-nymph, although the name must go back to the early time when special reverence was paid to the oak. See Pausanias X. 32. 6 regarding nymphs born from other trees, but especially from oaks.

**267, 268.** These verses have been suspected, partly because of the asyndeton (the omission of conjunctions). Gemoll avoids this with an unmetrical reading. It would be easy to correct this to a standard reading, but the asyndeton of **hestas'** (they stand) is excused by the start of the parenthesis. The pronoun **he** (her/it) has also caused offense; it is unique as a plural, but Pindar's use of **heas** for a plural subject seems to justify it. It is possible the writer copied passages like *Odyssey* 4. 355. See also Brugmann on Homeric textual criticism.

**<term>Ēlibatoi</term> <gloss>High/Precipitous</gloss>:** In Homer, this obscure word is found only in connection with rocks and is taken to mean "abrupt" or "precipitous," as in the *Hymn to Hermes* 404 or the *Hymn to Pan* 10. In the *Odyssey* 9. 243 and Hesiod, it is an epithet for a movable stone. There is a further extension of meaning in Hesiod's *Theogony* 483, describing a "deep" cave. In other later texts, it is applied to towers or stakes. We need not suspect the use of the word here as applied to trees.

Since it has been shown how both of these come to be, as we have already discussed. For it would be ridiculous, said I, but nevertheless, since we have gone through them as clearly as possible to see that these things are so, one must not grow weary. By Zeus, he said, one must not shrink from it at all. Come then, said I, so that you may see how many forms vice has, as it seems to me worthy of being seen. I will follow, he said, just keep speaking. And so, it appears to me as if from a high watchtower, since we have ascended so high in our argument, that there is one form of virtue, but infinite forms of vice. And of these, there are four that are worthy of mention. How do you mean? he said. Just as many as are the modes of government that have specific forms, so too do the modes of the soul seem to be. And how many were there? First of all, I said, of the governments, and of the soul as well. Speak, he said, which ones? I said, I mean that this one which we have discussed is the first form of government, though it would be called by different names. For if one person among those who rule excels, it would be called a kingship, and if there are more, an aristocracy. True, he said. This one, my friend, is one, for neither a multitude nor a single individual, having been properly trained and educated as we have discussed, will disturb the laws of the city that are worthy of note. # THE REPUBLIC OF PLATO, OR CONCERNING JUSTICE, FIFTH DISCOURSE.

<note>A woodcut depicts a pastoral landscape where several figures in classical robes are gathered near a portico, engaged in an earnest philosophical discussion.</note>

I joined such a city to that government, and I rightly call it so, and again I spoke of the others as faulty, just as this one is correct, concerning the administration of cities and the construction of the character of the soul for private individuals, being four in number in their wickedness. Which of these will you name? And I will speak of them in succession, as they appeared to me to transition from one to another. And Polemarchus (for he was sitting a little further away from Adeimantus), extending his hand and taking hold of his cloak, pulled him toward himself by the shoulder, and leaning forward, spoke some words, of which we heard nothing else but this: Shall we let him go, he said, or what shall we say? By all means, said Adeimantus, do not let him off. And I said, what specifically are you not letting me off from? From what you said, he replied, what do you think? It seems to us that you are trying to shirk, and that you are attempting to steal away the most important part of the argument, so that you do not have to discuss it, fearing that it might be easily refuted: that in the city, the women and children of those within the city will be common among friends. Did I not speak correctly, Adeimantus? Yes, he said, but this "correctly" needs to be established by argument, just as the other things were. What is the nature of this community? For there would be many ways it could be, but you are not saying which one you mean, though we have been waiting for a long time, expecting that you would not pass over the matter of procreation, how they will procreate in the city, and how they will raise those born, and this whole community of women and children that you speak of. For we think it matters a great deal to the whole of the government whether it is done correctly or not. Now, therefore, since you are taking up another government before discussing these things sufficiently, we have decided, he said, not to let you go until you have gone through all these things just like the others. And Glaucon said, consider me also a partner in this vote. Certainly, said Thrasymachus, consider these things as settled by all of us, Socrates. What have you done, said I, by taking hold of me? You are spinning the argument again, as if from the beginning, about the government of the city, which I was happy to have finished, content if anyone had accepted these things as they were said then. You do not know what a swarm of arguments you are stirring up, which I had then put aside so as not to hear them. Yes, I said, but they are moderate ones. They are moderate, Socrates, said Glaucon, for a life that has reason is a search for the whole truth. But let our concerns be; do not grow weary in questioning us about the cities. What you think is just, what is the community for our guardians, both concerning children and women, and the feeding of those still young, during the time between birth and education, which seems the most arduous. Tell us, therefore, in what manner these things are to be.

It is not easy, Adeimantus, I said, to divide these things. For there is even more disbelief in them than in those we discussed before. For they are not only disbelieved as being possible, but even if one were to agree that they would be best for the city, they are still disbelieved. Therefore, a certain hesitation hinders me, lest the argument might seem to be merely a wish, my dear friend.

Do not hesitate, he said. For those who will hear are not ignorant, nor are they disbelieving, nor are they ill-disposed. And I said, my best friend.

20 Over all the earth were they scattered and *driven* by lawless men.
For the heaven ceased to drop rain upon the earth,
21 The fountains were stayed, the everlasting fountains *that spring* out of the great depths *and* from the high mountains: because there was none among them that did righteousness and judgement.
From their ruler to <margin><sup>10</sup> *Gr. and*</margin> the vilest of the people, they were <sup>10</sup> altogether sinful.
22 The king was a transgressor, and the judge was disobedient, and the people sinful.

---

23 Behold, O LORD, and raise up unto them their king, the son of David, in the time which thou, O God, knowest, that he may reign over Israel thy servant;
24 And gird him with strength that he may break in pieces them that rule unjustly.

<note>The waters will fail, and the rivers will dry up. 4 Esdras vi. 24: And the veins of the fountains will stand still. *Testament of Levi* 4: while the waters are drying up.</note>

**doing righteousness and judgement.** Compare Ezekiel xviii. 5: "And the man who shall be righteous, who does judgement and righteousness," Psalm cxviii. (cxix.) 121: "I have done judgement and righteousness."

**from ruler... to the lowest of the people.** A very probable instance of a Hebrew idiom imperfectly understood; 'from their prince to the very least of the people,' meaning both their prince and the dregs of the mob. Compare Jonah iii. 5: "from their great ones to their small ones." Very possibly "to" <note>original: "ἕως"</note> should be supplied here; in xviii. 13 it was omitted by manuscript A and by older editors. The idiom in the <term>LXX</term> <gloss>Septuagint; the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</gloss> is generally given by "from...and to" <note>original: "ἀπὸ...καὶ ἕως"</note> (compare Exodus ix. 25, Joshua vi. 21, 1 Samuel xv. 3).

Geiger, who also explains the difficulty of the passage as due to a misapprehension of the Hebrew preposition "from" <note>original: "מן"</note>, connects "from their ruler" <note>original: "ἀπὸ ἄρχοντος αὐτῶν"</note> with the previous clause, 'No one practiced more than their prince.'

**22 the king.** The Asmonean Prince, referring to Hyrcanus II. or Aristobulus II.

**in disobedience.** Four of the manuscripts give this reading in place of 'in truth' <note>original: "ἐν ἀληθείᾳ"</note>, which was so unintelligible that Hilgenfeld's conjectural insertion of 'not' <note>original: "οὐκ"</note> was accepted by Fritzsche, Wellhausen ('in corruptibility'), and Pick, while Geiger suggested 'in impiety' <note>original: "ἐν ἀσεβείᾳ"</note>.

'Disobedience' <note>original: "ἀπείθεια"</note> is not found in the <term>LXX</term> <gloss>Septuagint</gloss>, but 'to disobey' <note>original: "ἀπειθεῖν"</note> is not uncommon; for example, Isaiah i. 23: 'your rulers disobey' (Symmachus: 'disobedient'), iii. 8.

<column-break/>

**23** The Psalmist has described, in the most moving terms he can employ, the state of decay into which the Jewish polity had fallen. To his mind there is only one possible remedy for it: the King promised long before, of the true ancient kingly line.

For the wording of the appeal many parallels can be cited. The promise originally made to David is in 2 Samuel vii. 12. In Jeremiah xxx. 9 we have 'I will raise up to them David their king' <note>original: "τὸν Δ. βασιλέα αὐτῶν ἀναστήσω αὐτοῖς"</note>. Compare Ezekiel xxxiv. 23, xxxvii. 25; and, as perhaps the earliest in date, Amos ix. 11: 'I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen' <note>original: "ἀναστήσω τὴν σκηνὴν τοῦ Δ. τὴν πεπτωκυῖαν"</note>.

**the time which thou knowest.** Compare Zechariah xiv. 7: 'that day shall be known to the LORD.' A reference to the old promise is indicated.

**24 gird** <note>original: "ὑπόζωσον"</note> occurs once in 2 Maccabees and in Acts xxvii. 17. The usual <term>LXX</term> <gloss>Septuagint</gloss> expression is 'to gird with strength' <note>original: "περιζωννύναι δύναμιν"</note>, Psalm xviii. 38, 43. In Isaiah xi. the Messiah is girded with righteousness and faithfulness.

**break in pieces.** Compare Numbers xxiv. 17: 'he shall break in pieces the leaders of Moab.' The corrupt Sadducean princes are to be cast down.

§. 22. For this reason, God also deems Er “wicked” <note>original: "πονηρὸν οἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς" - Genesis 38:7</note> and puts him to death, even without an obvious cause. For He is not ignorant that our fleshy mass—our body (for <term>Er</term> <gloss>a Hebrew name</gloss> is interpreted as "fleshy")—is wicked and plots against the soul, and is always dead and lifeless. For what else does each of us do but act as a corpse-bearer, with the soul raising up the body from itself and carrying it without struggle?

And consider, if you will, the strength of the soul. The strongest athlete would not be able to carry his own statue for a short time, yet the soul often carries the man’s statue for up to a hundred years without tiring. God did not kill the body just now; He made it dead from the beginning. It is wicked by nature, as I said, and a plotter against the soul, but it does not appear so to everyone, only to God and to anyone who is a friend of God. For Scripture says, “Er was wicked before the Lord.” <note>original: "Ἐναντίον γὰρ, φησὶ, κυρίου πονηρὸς Εῒρ."</note> For when the mind contemplates heavenly things and is initiated into the mysteries of the Lord, it judges the body to be wicked and hostile. But when it departs from the investigation of divine matters, it considers the body its friend, relative, and brother. Therefore, it takes refuge in things friendly to it. For this reason, the soul of an athlete and that of a philosopher differ. The athlete refers everything to the well-being of the body and would even sacrifice the soul itself for its sake, being a lover of the body. The philosopher, being a lover of the good, cares for that which lives within him—the soul—and disregards the body, which is a corpse, aiming only that the best part, the soul, may not be harmed by its wicked and dead shackles.

For He did not kill it now, but from the beginning He fashioned the body as dead. It is wicked by nature, as I said, and an enemy to the soul, but it is not apparent to all, only to God, and to anyone who is a friend of God. But the philosopher, being a lover of the good, cares for the living thing within himself, the soul, and disregards the body, which is dead, aiming only at this: that the best part, the soul, might not be led astray by its evil and dead bondsman.

**23** The Psalmist has described, in the most moving terms he can employ, the state of decay into which the Jewish polity had fallen. To his mind there is only one possible remedy for it: the King promised long before, of the true ancient kingly line.

For the wording of the appeal many parallels can be cited. The promise originally made to David is in 2 Sam. vii. 12. In Jer. xxx. 9 we have 'I will raise up to them David their king' <note>original: "τὸν Δ. βασιλέα αὐτῶν ἀναστήσω αὐτοῖς"</note>. Cf. Ezek. xxxiv. 23, xxxvii. 25; and, as perhaps the earliest in date, Amos ix. 11 'I will raise up the tabernacle of David that has fallen' <note>original: "ἀναστήσω τὴν σκηνὴν τοῦ Δ. τὴν πεπτωκυῖαν"</note>.

**the time which thou knowest** <note>original: "καιρὸν ὃν οἶδας"</note>. Cf. Zech. xiv. 7 that day is known to the Lord <note>original: "ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη γνωστὴ τῷ Κυρίῳ"</note>. A reference to the old promise is indicated.

**24 gird** <note>original: "ὑπόζωσον"</note> occurs once in 2 Macc. and in Acts xxvii. 17. The usual <term>LXX</term> <gloss>Septuagint</gloss> expression is 'to gird with strength' <note>original: "περιζωννύναι δύναμιν"</note>, Ps. xviii. 38, 43. In Is. xi. the Messiah is girded with righteousness and faithfulness.

**break in pieces** <note>original: "θραῦσαι"</note>. Cf. Num. xxiv. 17 'he shall break the leaders of Moab' <note>original: "θραύσει τοὺς ἀρχηγοὺς Μωάβ"</note>. The corrupt Sadducean princes are to be cast down.

Four of the seven veils are the passions, three are the various forms of delusion and ignorance. This is how Evagrius distinguishes them elsewhere. He speaks of the passions as follows: "as the knife circumcises the physical Jews, so the commandments of God circumcise the spiritual ones." Concerning the circumcision of ignorance, he says: "the stone knife is the teaching of Christ, which circumcises the reason that is wrapped in passions into true knowledge." There he speaks of the painful knife, here of the stone, because purification from the passions is associated with more toil and pain than instruction, even though both are necessary for mutual perfection. Paul also teaches two types of circumcision. "In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh in the circumcision of Christ" (Col. 2:11). There he speaks of the circumcision of the passions. Of the circumcision of ignorance, he writes: "to this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts; but when one of them turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (II Cor. 3:15), and we are the circumcision, who worship God in spirit (Phil. 3:3) and the circumcision of the heart (is what matters)" (Rom. 2:29). In the words "four of them are on the sixth day," the sixth day is a symbol of bodily labors and hardships and of the crucifixion; Israel worked six days and then rested. Against the passions common to our human nature—gluttony, lust, anger, and, linked to all, ambition, all <margin>175ᵇ</margin> at once passions of the body and the soul—the asceticism of body and soul helps, namely voluntary poverty, abstinence, mildness, humility. "The rest on the eighth day" refers to the veils of ignorance. Regarding them, he teaches that without the grace of the Spirit, which was given as a down payment at Pentecost and continues to be given from then on, no human being can be completely freed from the veil of delusion so that the light of truth may rise within him. Those four passions can sometimes be conquered by someone through persistent asceticism; however, no one can completely cast off the ignorance of delusion without the teaching of Christ and the grace of the Spirit, so that they may overcome the three types of demonic delusion that have been distributed throughout all heresies. Thus Evagrius himself speaks of the types of general delusion: "of the heretics, some have gone astray in the first knowledge of natures, others in the second, others again have derailed in the knowledge of the Trinity." Until a human being is purified of these three types of spiritual darkness through laborious, constant study accompanied by prayer, and has completely put off the old man, who is "corrupt through deceitful lusts," they will not be enlightened by the knowledge of faith, so that they might see the light and be called an "Israel of God." Cf. Chap. 57. These are the three circumcisions on the eighth day, which is a symbol of Sunday, which is simultaneously the first and eighth day, on which the children were circumcised. These are the four circumcisions of the sinful passions | which (?) the one who has gone out of the paradise of his nature and divided himself into four rivers and wrapped the world in a threefold evil of ignorance and sowed his weed seeds in three distinct ways waters and rears in man. <margin>176ᵃ</margin> I have treated this chapter in detail in the other book; I proved there that there are four veils of the passions, which hold the immature soul wrapped up like coats and thick skins (Gen. 3:21). When the reason makes its way out of them, it then beholds the light of the three types of knowledge. The seven walls of the curse (Josh. 6) burst, and the enslaved soul is made free by Jesus from the service of the seven nations (Deut. 7:1).

Of the circumcision of ignorance, he writes: "to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts; but when one of them turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away" (II Cor. 3:15), "and we are the circumcision, who worship God in spirit" (Phil. 3:3), and "the circumcision of the heart (is what matters)" (Rom. 2:29). In the words "four of them are on the sixth day," the 6th day is a symbol of physical labors and hardships and of the crucifixion; Israel worked for six days and then rested. Against the passions common to our human nature—gluttony, lust, anger, and, connected with all, vainglory, all <margin>175ᵇ</margin> being simultaneously passions of the body and soul—the asceticism of body and soul helps, namely voluntary poverty, temperance, gentleness, humility. "The rest on the 8th day" refers to the coverings of ignorance. Regarding them, he teaches that without the grace of the Spirit, which was given as a down payment at Pentecost and is given further from that point on, no human can be completely freed from the covering of delusion so that the light of truth may arise in him. Someone may sometimes conquer those 4 passions through persevering asceticism; but no one can completely cast off the ignorance of delusion without the teaching of Christ and the grace of the Spirit, such that he overcomes the three types of demonic delusion that have spread throughout all heresies. Thus Euagrius himself speaks of the types of general delusion: "of the heretics, some have gone astray in the first knowledge of natures, others in the second, others have again derailed in the knowledge of the Trinity." Until a person is cleansed of these three types of spiritual darkness through laborious, constant study accompanied by prayer, and has completely put off the old man who is corrupted by the "lusts of error," he is not illuminated by the knowledge of faith, so that he beholds the light and is called an "Israel of God." Cf. ch. 57. These are the three circumcisions on the eighth day, which is a symbol of the Sunday that is simultaneously the first and eighth day, on which the children were circumcised. These are the four circumcisions of the sinful passions | which (?) he waters and nurtures in man, he who <margin>176ᵃ</margin> has gone out from the paradise of his nature and divided himself into four rivers, and has shrouded the world with a threefold evil of ignorance, and has sown his weed-seed in a threefold different manner. I have treated this chapter in detail in the other book; I have proven there that there are four coverings of the passions, which keep the immature soul wrapped up like coats and thick skins (Gen. 3:21). When the reason extracts itself from them, then it beholds the light of the three types of knowledge. The seven walls of the curse (Josh. 6) burst, and the enslaved soul is freed by Jesus from the service of the seven nations (Deut. 7:1).

When Hananiah, the nephew of Rabbi Joshua, went down into exile, he began to intercalate years <note>adding a leap month to the lunar calendar</note> and fix the festivals <note>the calendar months</note> outside the Land of Israel. They sent two scholars after him: Rabbi Yose ben Kifara and the grandson of Zechariah ben Kabutal. He said to them, "Why have you come?" They answered him, "We have come to study Torah." He began to praise them, saying, "These men are great scholars, and they are the sons of great scholars, and our ancestors served in the Temple."

When Zechariah ben Kabutal voiced an opinion on a point of law that appeared strained to him, Hananiah began to declare things ritually impure while they declared them pure. He would forbid what they permitted; he would disqualify what they rendered fit. He then began to declare regarding them, "These men are men of vanity." They said to him, "You have already built, and you cannot now tear down. You have already fenced, and you cannot now break through. You declare pure, yet I forbid; you permit, yet I disqualify."

He said to him: We send three letters, one within thirty days, and one within [another] thirty days, and one within [another] thirty days; if he comes, that is good, and if not, we confiscate his property. Rabbi Hanina said: And when he stands for judgment, a person who did not say [he was] in judgment—we do not confiscate and we do not announce. You might find that Hanan and Rabbi Simeon both said one thing; just as you say the law follows Hanan, so too the law follows Rabbi Simeon. Rav said: If the borrower died, the lender takes an oath to the heirs; and even if the lender died, the heirs of the lender take an oath to the borrower. But if the borrower died first and afterward the lender [died], the lender has already become obligated to the children of the borrower to take an oath, and a man cannot bequeath his oath <note>original: "שבועתו"</note> to his children. Rabbi Yohanan heard and said: Let that man eat and rejoice. Rav Hiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav: A bond <note>original: "שטר"</note>...

### Mar'eh haPanim

**Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Bun said:** Meaning, since he said a minor is like an adult, meaning like an orphan who is a minor. For instance, as I have written inside, since in other places, as in [the tractates of] Ketubot and Gittin, all of it is corrupted in the printed versions... And I have already explained in Gittin there that the claim... I have come to a difficulty: Why would they give assessments for an adult, and [what is] the language of saying minors, whether for the poorest quality or for intermediate quality? For that which is written "whether for the poorest quality" is a dispute among the authorities... that regarding a creditor, he did not set his mind on orphans, and the property fell before the orphans... but regarding an adult... from the Torah, [it is collected] from the poorest quality for minors; we made a decree for adults, and such is the opinion of Rambam, may his memory be a blessing, there. And the simple reading of the words of Rambam, may his memory be a blessing... it seems so... that even [if the property] is from the mortgaged property before it comes to his hand... they are occupied with it through the orphans... and he collects for himself from the poorest quality. And I wrote there that one should not bring proof from the discussion here according to the opinion of Rabbeinu, may his memory be a blessing, for it is implied from the discussion that he is of the opinion that even regarding a creditor, there is a dispute between an orphan who is an adult and an orphan who is a minor... and there is no saying that the Talmud holds that it returns to the opinion that even regarding a creditor they dispute regarding intermediate quality... and it requires further study.

**Explain this** as [a case where someone] acted as a guarantor for him. See in the chapter "Hezkat," another law... it will be explained regarding this guarantor in his name, and it is explained there that he was...

**Liksa said before Rabbi Mana, etc.** On the face of it, one can learn from here regarding the matter of receiving testimony not in the presence of the litigant, as the opinion of the scholars... that he does not have a lawsuit against his fellow, and certainly not that they should accept [testimony] not in his presence, and all of his colleagues say that there is no [rule that] he has no claim... and if so, we confiscate property... one can explain that which Rabbi Hanina concludes, "And when he stands for judgment," etc., and if so, they have already received the testimony in his presence, in the standing for judgment, and we require the warning of the assets... in his presence before he speaks... and he concludes that we do not confiscate immediately... and we do not announce at first. And such is the case in the first chapter of Ketubot... and see above, chapter this... law 8... regarding what was explained concerning receiving testimony not in the presence of the litigant, and this appointment... and from here one can learn that if he had a debt before he stood for judgment, in such a case, they accept testimony not in his presence, as he says that we announce, and afterward if he does not appear immediately, they will do... and you have [no reason] to say [anything] greater than this, and as the conclusion of the authorities there.

**And so too** the law follows Rabbi Simeon. I have already written regarding this in Ketubot... that... the law follows Rabbi Simeon.

**Rabbi Yohanan heard and said: Let that man eat and rejoice.** Rabbi Yohanan, who held like Rabbi Simeon that if the lender died [and] this oath... and it has already been explained...

I wish to write here a portion of the introduction to the <term>Alfasi</term> <gloss>a prominent medieval halakhic compendium by Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</gloss>, and within it, I will also clarify some matters concerning faith as they appear to my humble opinion, according to the limits of my intellect and my meager understanding, remembering days of old.

At the beginning of my words, I wish to make known some of the foundations of religion and faith according to the way I have perceived his paths. For all the perfect paths are the paths upon which they [the Sages] stand, and in them are revealed the knowledge, morality, insight, and intellect of the past generations. In this, I will also explain to you the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, in their homilies and the narratives found in the <term>Talmud</term> <gloss>the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</gloss>. Every single one of these matters is worthy to be known and understood according to their truth, not according to their apparent meaning. Lest one who thinks or understands the words only according to their literal sense—or the simple meaning of statements that are not consistent with abstract reason—err, or err against true judgment. It is certain that goodness will be found in the interpretation of these mentioned matters, for these are the essence of the <term>Torah</term> <gloss>the Law/Pentateuch</gloss> and the <term>mitzvot</term> <gloss>commandments</gloss>.

The Rabbi also said in his introduction to <term>Berakhot</term> <gloss>the first tractate of the Talmud</gloss>, and these are his words: "And this is what is written, 'On the Sabbath day, holy to the Lord' <note>original: "ביום השבת קדש ה' לו"</note>... 'for in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed' <note>original: "כי ששת ימים עשה ה' את השמים ואת הארץ וביום השביעי שבת וינפש"</note>." And the Rabbi, of blessed memory, wrote: "Behold, Scripture appears to say that the Holy One, blessed be He, as it were, rested on the seventh day, etc. But in truth, this is not the judgment, for the Name, may He be blessed, is not subject to weariness or fatigue, and heaven forbid that He should need rest or refreshing. Rather, it is all by way of metaphor and analogy, according to our limited grasp and understanding."

This is the matter referred to in the Torah, and it is written therein, that we have seen in many places the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, in their homilies and their statements, which point to strange things in their literal and apparent meaning. Yet their explanations and their inwardness are profound and are true matters regarding the paths of faith and intellectual truths. It is proper for us to recognize and understand these matters with our intellect, lest our words be as those of fools, God forbid. What is good for a person to see is that he should examine the commentaries and books that interpret these matters according to straight reason. Behold, such things have appeared in writing, and those who understand will understand. All these things are the words of the living God.

The famous sage, the author of the <term>Akedah</term> <gloss>referring to Rabbi Isaac Arama's philosophical commentary on the Torah</gloss>, of blessed memory, also wrote in the first gate that everything depends on the understanding mind. Thus, the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, are interpreted in many places, for heaven forbid that they would write things that have no taste or scent, God forbid. He concluded: "May the Name, may He be blessed, in His abundant mercy, guide us in the path of truth, and teach us Torah and knowledge, and place in our hearts insight and intellect to understand, learn, teach, observe, and do all the words of His Torah in truth and integrity. Amen, Selah." This is what I wished to mention here regarding the matter of some of the words of our Sages, the homilists, and regarding faith as previously stated.

Way of Life: Reproof and Moral Instruction

And now, the sixteenth section has been completed in its number and order. With His wisdom, the Sages of the Talmud have stated that one should only believe the good of them. And now, after these sections—short and long—we shall come to the interpretation, like the season of the Creator of light. I will turn my hand to the laws mentioned above in the verse, "For even this over against that" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:14</note> (meaning the sections and the laws of the shofar mentioned), and I have, with the help of Heaven, explained them (meaning the aforementioned laws of the shofar) according to the intent of the sections mentioned shortly hereafter. The general intent is one: "He instructs sinners in the way" <note>Psalms 25:8</note>, according to the value of the sections mentioned, both short and long.

## The law is that the shofar of Rosh Hashanah is [commanded] to be of a ram, etc., as mentioned in the section <note>referring to a previous section of the work, abbreviated as "Hatz"a"H"</note>, which is called the "penitent's shofar" due to the two reasons mentioned there. This appears to me:

<margin>And this is called a complete penitent, as the Sages said (in the last chapter of Yoma): What is a complete penitent? For example, one who is presented with the opportunity for a sin the first, second, and third time, and he is exempt regarding that same episode (this is the strength of youth), and with the same woman, and in the same place (this is the strength of the sin). Therefore, they meant by this, in his youth and sharpness, and he is not exempt from the sin due to old age or weakness of strength, but he is strong in conquering his inclination and refrains; this is what they meant by this.</margin>

The intention of the Sages in what they said here, "The shofar of Rosh Hashanah" (and calling it the shofar of Rosh Hashanah, because it is the appointed time of the year to grasp one's deeds and return to God, for repentance preceded the creation of man, as written inside, and see that Rosh Hashanah is the beginning of the Ten Days of Repentance, so it is fitting to compare the penitent to the shofar of Rosh Hashanah), its mitzvah is with a ram. The essence of the mitzvah of a penitent is when he returns from his evil way, that he returns in the days of his youth in his strength and might. And the "ram" mentioned here is from the expression "ram that butts" <note>Daniel 8:3</note>, and from the expression "and the rams of the land he took" <note>Ezekiel 17:13</note>, and from the expression "is there not strength in my hand" <note>Genesis 31:29</note>, which explains that all of these are strength and might. They hinted at the strength of the powers, and also at the strength of the sin. This means that that same sin in which he stumbled in his youth is available before him, and he desires it, and it is in his power to commit it as before, yet he is strong to conquer his inclination and refrains from it because of repentance, not because of a failure of strength. For it is completely different when his inclination overcomes him and says to him, "Let us do it this time," and he stands up and answers, "What you have done already, etc."

## And it appears to me
That this is what they intended by what they interpreted regarding the verse, "Happy is the man who fears the Lord" (Psalms 112:1), and it was brought above in the section: "A man, and not a woman." Rav Amram said, "Happy is he who performs repentance while he is a man." And everyone says, "Happy is he who overcomes his inclination like a man." Rashi explains: "When he is a man, at a time when he is burning with heat," meaning he hastens to extinguish it, or he came before the days of old age like a strong man. And it is possible that Rabbi Levi did not come to argue with Rav, but to explain the words of Rav. He said, what Rav meant by "Happy is he who performs repentance while he is a man," his intention was as we said, when he is a youth, as mentioned. He did not speak only of the strength of the physical powers, but he spoke of the strength of the sin, that it is similar to standing before an enkindled fire, and he is not in this because of compulsion but because of fear. And he is not a man who pursues his inclination as at the beginning, but he is strong, conquering his inclination because of the fear of sin. And this is what Rabbi Levi said, "that he overcomes his inclination, etc." For this, it is worthy to say of him, "Happy is the man who fears the Lord," a complete penitent. And Rav, who said "when he is a man," by which he meant "in youth," said "Happy is the man" who possesses two strengths: the strength of youth, and the strength of conquering his inclination at that same episode, and with that same woman, etc. And this is the general principle hinted at in the word "ram" (ail), which is an expression of force and strength. And there is an extra level in this: the strength of the ram (regarding the powers), and the strength of the man (regarding the sin itself, in that same episode and that same woman, etc.). And even if he bows his desire in this, according to our way, the penitent must humble himself and be bowed, to bend his pride and haughtiness, and to consider his soul as dust for all, and this is the essence of repentance as above in the section on humility. And the Sages came to inform us here by saying, "The shofar of Rosh Hashanah, its mitzvah is with a ram," and "bent" (kofuf), that he should lower himself. The mitzvah of the shofar and the operation through which the penitent (likened to the shofar) will reach the highest level for the World to Come, is that which we sound with a ram and "bent," according to the way mentioned shortly.

### And in the measure
Of the penitent's repentance, he will reach a level of greatness. This is a very essential matter, for the perfectly righteous cannot stand in this great place, as was mentioned in the section on humility. And this is why the penitent reaches such a great level, though others are below him. It is already explained in the first section that our level is the World to Come and above it, and it is also explained in the third section that the level of one penitent is greater and higher in the World to Come than the level of another penitent.

## And this is what he said, "And post-factum (b'di-avad) all shofars are valid, whether straight or bent."
This means even if it is not from a ram and not bent. And he means "not from a ram" according to our way, that is, even one who did not repent in his youth when he was in his force and strength, which is the superior repentance as above, but waited to repent until his old age. That is, the strength of the vitality of youth and the strength of the sin have passed and gone, meaning that that same sin, in its episode, place, and woman, is not available before him as before. And he means by "not bent," that is, he did not humble himself in his strength to bow his pride, to cause that hard pride to be completely lowered, as in the section on humility, but only removed from himself the pride and spirit, and also the excessive pride that was in him previously, which led him to sin as it is said, "And your heart will be haughty and you will forget the Lord your God." He now stands in the middle, in humility, and not having lowered himself as much as the first, but he still has a level in the World to Come, and this is the fifth level mentioned in the third section. And this is what he said, "And post-factum all shofars are valid." And this is what appears to me as to what the Sages intended in the law of the ram and the bent shofar. According to our way, in addition to what was said above: "Prepare before Me a shofar of a ram so that I may remember for you the Binding of Isaac, and that I may account it to you as if you had bound yourselves before Me," and "bent," so that they may bend their hearts to prayer.

# And they said: "Except for that of a cow, which is invalid in every respect."
And its explanation: if it is from a cow, even post-factum, it is invalid. The Sages hinted here, according to our way, at those people who are like the red cow, characterized by the redness of sin. And if they remain red—meaning due to sins—even until old age and hoary hair, they do not repent, or they do not repent due to pride and haughtiness. For everyone who is haughty is elevated from performing repentance, because repentance depends on submission as mentioned in the section on humility, and it is said regarding Ahab, "Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me?" and so on.

## And this is what he said:
(And it is not called in the Holy Tongue "shofar" but "horn" [keren]). For you already have the knowledge that the term "horn" is authority, as "My horn is exalted" <note>1 Samuel 2:1</note>, and also "the horn of His anointed," and "the horn of salvation." And it means that he who has not abandoned pride and authority does not set his heart to repent, as it is said, "And your heart will be haughty and you will forget the Lord your God," etc. Therefore, it is invalid even post-factum if it is the horn of pride, for pride does not let him repent, as above. And these are those of whom the Sages said: "The wicked, even at the entrance of Gehinnom, do not repent," and they die in their sin due to the horns of their pride.

## And they said "because":
So too the horns of most beasts, meaning wild, predatory beasts—these are the wicked who are like the beasts of the forest, as seen in the chapter on merit. They are all one, meaning they do not have a heart of flesh but a heart of stone and bone, and they harden their hearts from performing repentance all their days, forever, until they die in their sins.

## And this is what he said:
"And their 'ail' (ram) is bent..."—meaning they do not remember in the depths of their hearts the day of death, and they are not fearful, not worried, and not sad about it. Just as the Sages said (in Tractate Shabbat) regarding the verse, "There are no pangs for their death" (Psalms 73:4), the Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is not enough for the wicked that they are not fearful and sad about the day of death, but their heart is healthy for them as if, etc. Therefore, they are completely invalid for the World to Come (just as this shofar is invalid even post-factum), and they are the heretics who do not believe in the Day of Judgment and the providence of his body and soul to punish, and they are placed among the generations mentioned at the end of the third section.

# "All sounds are valid in the shofar"
This explains the corrections of the sounds. These sounds, meaning even if the sound is light in the whole Torah, the Lord will consider it in His mercy. Even if he has committed many iniquities, and says, "What will the performance of the mitzvah avail me if I have committed many sins?", he should perform many mitzvot, as it is said, "For with strategies you shall wage your war" <note>Proverbs 24:6</note>, and the Sages interpreted this: a person whose burdens are upon him, they should perform sounds against him.

<summary>This passage interprets the legal requirements of the shofar for Rosh Hashanah as a symbolic guide for the process of repentance, emphasizing the importance of youth, strength of will, humility, and the rejection of pride.</summary>
