# Introduction and Tributes

This introduction was intended to mark the twentieth anniversary of the founding of the Egyptian Institute for Islamic Studies in Madrid, which publishes and sponsors this journal. This preface was prepared to record the research the Institute has undertaken during this period, and the goals it has achieved with the assistance of many Spanish professors and Orientalist scholars in universities across the world. It serves as an analytical pause to survey the path toward the future and to attribute credit to those who deserve it. If the magnificent history of Islamic Spain is a shared fortune between us and the Spanish—they possessed the place, and we together possessed the time—then the spirit of research and scientific cooperation has provided this Institute, from its very first day, with genuine friendships that span the length and breadth of the Spanish land.

The introduction began by recalling a great day from the legacy of the prominent Arab scholar Dr. Taha Hussein, when he secured from the Council of Ministers, prior to the revolution, the decision to establish this Institute. We, the students of the Egyptian educational mission, welcomed him when he arrived in Madrid. He delivered the opening speech on the eleventh day of November in the year nineteen hundred and fifty, before a large gathering of university men, senior officials, and Spanish intellectuals.

Regimen for ripening agents: Warmth is regulated so that it matches the body's natural heat, allowing a certain softening for them. Among those are in the first grade: fomentation with warm water and application of a poultice with wheat flour, or barley and wheat flour, and honey is masticated. In this, bread with pitch or wax and saffron and powdered frankincense, and pitch with oil of roses, or lard, or a poultice of mallow, mucilage, and flaxseed. And again, a poultice of sweet, fatty, and moist figs, or with barley flour, and barley flour again, and specifically if wild hyssop or marjoram is placed in it, or collected with water in which they are boiled with a little salt, not excessive. And sometimes fat or oil is placed in it, or in that, two parts of glue of the whites <note>likely egg whites</note>. And medicines composed of <term>vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver/mercury</gloss>, <term>passis</term> <gloss>raisins</gloss>, <term>thure</term> <gloss>frankincense</gloss>, <term>galbanum</term>, <term>myrrh</term>, <term>laudanum</term>, <term>resin</term>, <term>butter</term>, <term>mastic</term>, <term>hyssop</term>, and the root of the squirting cucumber and the root of dragon's tongue. And the poultice of Galen with oil of spikenard without wax, and specifically when this poultice is dissolved in oil, it becomes the <term>didimoa</term> <gloss>a specific plaster</gloss> and the <term>basilicon</term> <gloss>a royal plaster</gloss>. And among the good things for this is the medicine of <term>marchasite</term> <gloss>pyrite/ore</gloss> stone with ammoniac, which is placed on top until it falls off by itself.

Regimen for exitures <note>abscesses/lesions</note> when they are ripe. Ch. 29.
When you find an exitura with thick skin where, despite ripening, one does not expect it to burst, and there are veins, cords, and nerves there, then it is ordered that you lance it, because if you leave it, the pus will spoil, corrupt, and corrode the flesh and the fibers of the nerves. That will indeed be more severe when it is near joints. And you, indeed, should seek the place of the pus with your lancing. And be careful that the lancing hole falls lower, unless it is not possible. And if that which is above the exitura is thick and you have cut it, then cut the hole only when you apply the plaster with that which is behind it, and if it has been thinned, then cut all of it lengthwise. And know that the place in which there is pus is declared by touch, and when you touch it with a finger, specifically observe with the other fingers, at least of the other hand, whether anything is expelled from it. And the place of the pus appears from the turning of the color towards whiteness, and it is ripe, and then it turns towards redness. And sometimes the place of the pus is inclined towards redness and yellowness when the pus is not good to be discerned by touch without sight, although sight is an aid. It is ordered, therefore, that in the incision you follow the natural lines of the ligatures, which are near the pus, unless there is a necessity, and in limbs diversified by the position of the fibers in length and in the place of the ligature. For if you have followed that in the lancing of an exitura that is on the forehead, the ligature will cause the skin of the forehead to fall onto the face. Rather, it is ordered that you vary the ligature. In those, however, that are like the groin, it is ordered that you go with the ligature in the width of the skin. And when you have lanced the exitura and extracted what is in it, then it is necessary that you take care to glue the skin to the flesh so that it does not break and harden and become such that it does not glue, whereby it becomes a sinus that does not cease to be filled, and it avoids the healing of the first exitura. And if it is necessary for you to use it, insert a probe onto whose head is an abrasive cloth with which you clean the inner edges, then make it adhere and preserve it with a ligature as we will say concerning the ligatures of sinuses and ulcers. It will be very suitable. And it is ordered that you observe in the lancing that which we said about the conditions: where to lance in the more ripe place and in the part longer and away from veins, arteries, and cords.

<column-break/>

Antyllus says: If an exitura is on the head, then its incision is made wide; and if it happens in the nose, we shall lance it equally with the size of the length of the nose. And if it is near the eye, we shall lance it with the lancing of the thread of a new moon and make the tortuosity downwards. If, however, it happens in the jaw, we shall cut it with an equal incision, when the composition of this place is equal, and that is known from the bodies of the <term>fennu</term> <gloss>chapters/sections</gloss>. After the ear, however, we lance it; all that are there we lance in length. He says: and if it is near the thighs, we shall lance it with a round lancing, and a round lancing indeed is that which catches with its grasp the length of the body and some of its width. He says: when this place is not lanced roundly, it is possible that materials aggregate in it and become fistulas. And it is also lanced that which is near the anus, because of the place of moisture that aggregates in it. And in the side and ribs, it is lanced by opening, but in the testicle and penis, equally, he says. And let us be ready always to ensure that the result follows the shape of the place as much as we can upon it. Groins and helpers are cut in length, and preserve it so that the nerves are not injured. And know that the lancing is diversified according to locations; when it is the eye, then its length is wide, similar to the position of the eye; and in the nose, it is with the length of the nose; and in the jaw, it is with the length of the jaw; and near the ear, it is cut equally, when the position of this place is equal, and that is known from the bodies of the <term>fennu</term> <gloss>chapters/sections</gloss>. After the ear, however, it is lanced equally in the arms and legs, and the thigh and penis, all equally, it is done in length; and it is done in the shoulders and in the back. In the groins and the lumbar region, when you place yourself for the lancing, take from the width also so that a sinus does not form in it, which would become a fistula. And it is done in that which is near the anus, take from the width also so that a sinus does not come to pass and become a fistula; and the testicles and penis, equally and in length; in the side and ribs, take in the width also so that it is transverse, as the position of the ribs is such, and the flesh that is over them. He says: consider always the position of the flesh and the fibers of the muscles, for they are not together ready except for this, that we lance with imitation of the place so that it does not come to pass that it is enclosed, and the place of healing becomes good, not thick. And in everything, dispose your study so that you do not cut an artery, nor a large vein, or a nerve, or the fibers of a muscle, and the lancing is done according to the size of the exitura. But if it is small and what is in it runs from one place, then cut it in one place; and if it is large, then lance it from the beginning, then insert your left index finger into it, and lance it where the head arrives, and then insert it also into the opening, and according to this until you arrive upon it. And if the exitura has a sufficient place from which it is possible for what is in it to exit, we shall lance it in that place; and if it is round, or has a figure such that what is in it does not exit by one lancing, we shall lance it in the inner part of itself in two or three places, according to the quantity that you know, for everything that aggregates in it runs in an hour. He says: let there be nothing of the exitura [that is] punctural, or a noble member, or a member near a bone, or in danger, [without] we hasten in the lancing, and sometimes we confirm for it the ripening lest something of these members is corrupted. I say, therefore, this is the regimen when we find no excuse for lancing. If, however, we hope that it might rupture by itself, we shall not lance; and similarly, if we hope that it might erupt through medicines that cause eruption: perhaps, indeed, we find in medicines causing eruption that which stands in the place of lancing. And many times the skin is lanced by some lancing, or something is taken from it, afterwards eruptions are placed upon it so that a lancing is made for it.

Abū Muḥammad ibn Durustawayh mentioned that he heard the *Kitāb al-‘Ayn* with this chain of transmission. **Regimen for exitures <note>abscesses/tumors</note> when they are mature. L.xxix.**
If you find an <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> with thick skin with maturation, for which an eruption is not expected, and there are veins and cords and nerves there, then it is necessary that you perforate it. For if you leave the pus, it will corrupt and corrode the skin and the filaments of the nerves, and that will be more vehement when it is near the joints. And you should seek the site of the pus with your perforation. And be careful that the hole of the perforation is lower, unless it is not possible. And if that which is above the <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> is thick, and you have cut it, then make the hole only when you apply the plaster with that which is after it; and if it is thinned, then cut all of it lengthwise. And know that the place in which there is pus is declared by touch, and when you touch it with a finger, you should specifically observe with the other fingers of the other hand whether anything is expelled from it. And the site of the pus appears by the decline of color to whiteness, and then it is mature, whereas it declines to redness. And sometimes the site of the pus is inclined to redness and yellowness when the pus is not good to sustain by touch without sight, although sight is helpful. Therefore, it is necessary that in the incision you obtain the natural lines of the binding, which are near the pus, except in case of necessity; and in limbs differentiated by the position of the filaments, [make the incision] in length and in the place of the binding. For if you follow that in the perforation of an <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> that is above the forehead, the binding of the skin of the forehead will fall upon the face; rather, it is necessary that you vary the binding. In those that are like in the groin, it is necessary that you go with the binding in the width of the skin. And when you have perforated the <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> and extracted what is in it, then it is necessary that you assist in gluing the skin with the flesh so that it does not rupture and harden and become such that it does not glue, whereby it becomes a <term>finus</term> <gloss>sinus</gloss> that does not cease to fill and flows with the threads of the first <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss>. And if it is necessary for you to use it, insert a probe upon the head of which is a rough cloth with which you clean those scrapings, then make it adhere and preserve it with a binding as we shall say concerning the bindings of cavities and ulcers; it will be very convenient. And it is necessary that you observe in the perforation that which we have said concerning the conditions, where you perforate in the more mature place and the part longer from veins, arteries, and cords.

<column-break/>

Antyllus says if the <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> is in the head, then its incision is made wide, and if it happens in the nose, we shall perforate it equal to the length of the nose. And if it is near the eye, we shall perforate it with a perforation like the head of a new moon and make a curvature downwards. But if it happens in the jaw, we shall cut it with an equal incision when the composition of this place is equal, and that is known from the bodies of the <term>fenu</term> <gloss>chapters/sections</gloss>. After the ear, however, we perforate all those in the groin in length. He says and if it is near the thighs, we shall perforate it with a round perforation; and a round perforation is indeed that which grasps with its grasp the length of the body, something of its width. He says when this place is not perforated roundly, it is possible that matters aggregate in it and become fistulas. And it is also perforated that which is near the anus, because of the place of humidity that aggregates in it. And in the side and ribs, it is perforated by opening; in the testicle, however, and the penis, in an equal [manner]. He says and let us be ready always so that the result is a figure of the place as much as we can upon it. Groins, however, and assistants are cut in length, and preserve so that the nerves are not injured. And know that the perforation is diversified according to the places, when [for example] it is the eye, then its length is wide according to the position of the eye; and in the nose, it is with the length of the nose; and in the jaw, it is with the length of the jaw; and near the ear, it is cut equally when the position of this place is equal, and that is known from the bodies of the <term>fenu</term> <gloss>chapters/sections</gloss>. After the ear, however, it is perforated equally in the arms and legs, and the thigh and the penis, all equally, it is done in length; and it is done in the shoulders and in the back, but in the groins and <term>lubaecell</term> <gloss>armpits</gloss>, you will take for the perforation that which also takes from the width, so that a sinus does not occur in it which becomes a fistula. And it is done in that which is near the anus, take from the width also, so that a sinus does not come and a fistula is made. And the testicles and penis, equally and in length; in the side and ribs, take in width also, so that it is transverse, since the position of the ribs is such, and the flesh that is upon them. He says always consider the position of the flesh and the filaments of the muscles, since they are not ready except for this, that we perforate with imitation of the place so that a sinus does not arrive and the place of flesh-growth becomes good, not thick. And do in every arrangement your study so that you do not cut an artery, nor a large vein, or nerve, or the filaments of the muscle, and let the perforation be according to the size of the <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss>. But if it is small and that which is in it runs from one place, then cut it in one place; and if it is large, then perforate it from the beginning, then introduce your left index finger into it, and perforate it where the head arrives, and then introduce it also into the opening of it, and according to this until you arrive upon it. And if there is a sufficient place for the <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> from which it is possible for that which is in it to exit, we shall perforate it in that place; and if it is round or has a figure so that what is in it does not exit by one perforation, we shall perforate it in the inner part of itself in two places or three, according to the quantity that you know, since everything that aggregates in it runs into the <term>boza</term> <gloss>hollow/cavity</gloss>. He says if the <term>exitura</term> <gloss>abscess</gloss> is a puncture or a noble limb or a limb near a bone or a <term>piniculo</term> <gloss>little membrane/nerve cluster</gloss>, we shall hasten in the perforation, and before it is firm, for its maturation might corrupt some of these limbs. I say therefore this is the regimen when we find no excuse for perforation. But if we hope that it might rupture by itself, we shall not perforate; and similarly, if we hope that it may erupt through medicines causing eruption; perhaps, indeed, we find in medicines causing eruption that which stands in the place of perforation. And often the skin is perforated by some perforation, or something is taken from it, afterward eruptions causing [the issue] are placed upon it so that a perforation is made for it.

# Introduction and Reflections

It was intended for this introduction to mark the passage of twenty years since the founding of the Egyptian Institute for Islamic Studies in Madrid, which publishes and sponsors this journal. This introduction was indeed prepared as a record of the research the Institute has undertaken during this period and the goals it has achieved with the assistance of many Spanish professors and scholars of Orientalism in universities around the world and beyond. It serves as a careful review that seeks a path toward the future and gives credit where it is due. If the magnificent history of Muslim Spain is a common lot between us and the Spaniards—they possessed the place, while we and they shared the time—then the spirit of research and scientific cooperation has provided this Institute, from its very first day, with genuine friendships spanning the length and breadth of the Spanish land.

The introduction began by recalling the history of a great day among the achievements of the renowned Arabist Dr. Taha Hussein, when he secured a decree from the Council of Ministers before the Revolution to establish this Institute. We, the students of the Egyptian Educational Mission, welcomed him when he arrived in Madrid, and he delivered the inaugural address on the eleventh of November in the year nineteen hundred and fifty, before a large gathering of university figures, senior officials, and Spanish intellectuals.

The situation is like that of rays and lights when they radiate from centers and circles spreading across the surface of water after it has been struck. When age and weakness overtake them, they begin to diminish from the extremities, yet the center remains preserved until God decrees the total extinction of the matter; only then does the center perish. If the state is overcome from its center, the remaining extremities and outer perimeter are of no use to it, and it dissolves instantly. For the center is like the heart from which the spirit radiates. If the heart is conquered and possessed, all the extremities are defeated. 

Observe this in the Persian state: its center was <term>al-Mada'in</term> <gloss>Ctesiphon</gloss>. When the Muslims conquered <term>al-Mada'in</term>, the rule of Persia collapsed entirely, and it did not help <term>Yazdgerd</term> that he retained control over parts of his peripheral kingdoms. The opposite was the case for the Roman state in the Levant. Since its center was Constantinople, and the Muslims took the Levant from them, they retreated to their centers in Constantinople. The loss of the Levant did not harm them, and their kingdom remained connected to that center until God decreed its extinction. 

Observe also the case of the Arabs at the beginning of Islam. When their solidarity was abundant, they conquered the land in the fastest time, then moved beyond that to what lies beyond, such as Sindh, Abyssinia, Africa, and the Maghreb, and then to Andalusia. But when they divided into portions across the kingdoms and frontier regions and settled them as garrisons, their numbers were exhausted by those distributions. They fell short of further conquests, and the expansion of Islam ceased and did not proceed further.

# Guai (The Break-Through)
"Proclaiming it in the king's court. Sincere calls, there is danger. Informing from one's own city. It is not advantageous to resort to weapons. It is advantageous to have a place to go."

## Tuan Zhuan (Commentary on the Judgments)
Guai means to break through. It is the firm breaking through the yielding. It is vigorous and joyful. Breaking through while remaining in harmony. "Proclaiming it in the king's court" signifies the yielding [line] riding atop the five firm [lines]. "Sincere calls, there is danger" means its danger will therefore be luminous. "Informing from one's own city; it is not advantageous to resort to weapons" means that to rely on force is to reach an impasse. "It is advantageous to have a place to go" means the firm is growing and will ultimately prevail.

Kong Zhongda says: The king's court is the place where all officials reside. The noble person breaks through against the petty person, and therefore one may clearly and openly resolve the matter. This demonstrates ultimate justice without selfish concealment. To rely exclusively on martial ferocity and use this to resort to weapons is to value force to achieve victory. This is breaking through without harmony, and such a path leads to an impasse.

Wang Jiepu says: The yielding rides upon the five firm lines. The top-six line rides upon the firmness of the nine-five line. The multitude of yang lines are clustered near the five, [collectively] seeking to resolve the five.

# 含章可貞，以時發也；或從王事，知光大也。

二在地爻，正合乾坤之本位也。乾主九五，故於五言乾之大用，而九二止言乾德之美。坤主六二，故於二言坤之大用，而六五止言坤德之美。六二之直，即至柔而動剛也。六二之方，即至靜而德方也。其大即後得主而有常，含萬物而化光也。其不習无不利，即坤道其順乎承天而時行也。六二蓋全具坤德者。孔子懼人不曉六二何由兼有乾直，故解之曰：六二之動，直以方也。言坤動也，剛所以能直也。又懼人不曉六二何由无不利，故解之曰：地道光也。言地道主六二，猶乾之九五，言乃位乎天德也。

# Guai (Breakthrough)
Manifest it in the king’s court. Sincerity and warning of danger. Announce it from your own city. It is not advantageous to take up arms. It is advantageous to have a destination.

## Tuan Zhuan (Commentary on the Judgement)
*Guai* means to resolve. It is the strong resolving the weak. Being resolute yet joyous, making a decision while remaining harmonious. "Manifest it in the king’s court" because the weak one <note>the single yin line at the top</note> is riding upon five strong ones. "Sincerity and warning of danger" means its peril will lead to brightness. "Announce it from your own city, it is not advantageous to take up arms" means that if one values only force, one will reach an impasse. "It is advantageous to have a destination" means that as the strong lines grow, the matter will be brought to an end.

Kong Zhongda <note>Kong Yingda, 574–648 CE, a Tang dynasty scholar</note> says: The king’s court is the place where the hundred officials reside. The noble person makes decisions regarding the petty person, so one should openly and clearly resolve the matter. This shows utmost impartiality without hidden motives. To rely solely on might and ferocity, and to use this to take up arms, is to value strength in order to attain victory. This is being resolute without being harmonious; such a path leads to an impasse.

Wang Jiefu <note>Wang Anshi, 1021–1086 CE, a Song dynasty statesman and reformer</note> says: The weak one rides upon five strong ones. The top six <note>the sixth line from the bottom, which is a yin line</note> rides upon the strength of the nine five <note>the fifth line from the bottom, which is a yang line</note>. The multitude of yang lines are close to the five, personally deciding the five.

# "Containing beauty, one may be persevering," to be put forth at the proper time; "or following the king's affairs," knowing the greatness of its radiance.

The number two in the earthly hexagram <note>referring to the Kun hexagram</note> correctly corresponds to the fundamental position of the <term>Qian</term> <gloss>Creative/Heaven</gloss> and <term>Kun</term> <gloss>Receptive/Earth</gloss> principles. Because <term>Qian</term> is centered on the nine-five position, it speaks of the great application of <term>Qian</term>, while the nine-two position only speaks of the beauty of <term>Qian</term>'s virtue. Because <term>Kun</term> is centered on the six-two position, it speaks of the great application of <term>Kun</term>, while the six-five position only speaks of the beauty of <term>Kun</term>'s virtue. The "straightness" of the six-two position is precisely the state of being most yielding yet moving with strength. The "squareness" of the six-two position is precisely the state of being most still yet possessing a square virtue. Its "greatness" is precisely that of following others to take charge while maintaining constancy, containing all things, and radiating light through transformation. That "without practice, there is no unadvantageousness" means the way of <term>Kun</term> is compliant, supporting Heaven and acting according to the seasons. The six-two position fully embodies the virtue of <term>Kun</term>. Confucius feared that people might not understand how the six-two position could possess the straightness of <term>Qian</term>, so he explained it, saying: "The movement of the six-two position is straight and square." This means that when <term>Kun</term> moves, it is because of strength that it can be straight. He also feared that people might not understand why the six-two position has "no unadvantageousness," so he explained it, saying: "The way of the earth is radiant." This means the way of the earth resides in the six-two position, just as the nine-five position of <term>Qian</term> resides in the position of heavenly virtue. 

Cai Qing says: The way of the earth is the "straight and square" way. Its radiance is being straight, square, and great. By occupying the straight, square, and great, one is without practice yet encounters no disadvantage. Ye E'zhan says: Interpret "straight and square" as one concept. The movement of the six-two position is square, yet this is derived from what is stored within it—straightness. Because it is straight, what is manifested externally is square.

### Song

Emperor Gaozong possessed marvelous skill in both calligraphy and painting. His depictions of figures, landscapes, bamboo, and rocks possess a natural elegance. Even while amidst military campaigns, he did not abandon his brush and ink. Every time a painting was completed, he would order his eunuch attendants to take charge of it. If it was not bestowed upon a close minister, it was rewarded to an old veteran of merit. He cherished these works more than noble titles or gifts. On the spaces where he inscribed characters, he used the "Qian Hexagram" seal. In his later years, while residing in the Northern Palace, he used the "Seal of the Retired Emperor," the "Imperial Seal of the Deshou Palace," and the "Seal of the Imperial Treasury" for those works passed down to the world.

## Xian (Mutual Influence)

The first section of the Upper Canon establishes the positions of Qian (Heaven) and Kun (Earth), and thus the positions of the Father and Mother are fixed. Following these are Tun (Difficulty at the Beginning) and Meng (Youthful Folly). The interactions between the eldest, middle, and youngest sons form the hexagrams that serve as the guiding principles for the various Yang hexagrams of the Upper Canon. However, the themes of Thunder and Mountain had already begun in Tun and Meng, while Wind and Lake subsequently appeared in Xiao Chu (Small Restraint) and Lü (Treading). Thunder and Mountain follow Water; Wind and Lake follow Heaven. In between are Xu (Waiting), Song (Conflict), Shi (The Army), and Bi (Holding Together), which involve the four arrangements of Water-Heaven, Heaven-Water, Earth-Water, and Water-Earth.

## Xian (Mutual Influence)

The opening of the Upper Classic discusses Qian (Heaven) and Kun (Earth) establishing the positions of the cosmos; with the positions of the father and mother thus determined, the text follows with Zhun (Difficulty at the Beginning) and Meng (Youthful Folly). The three sons—eldest, middle, and youngest—interact to form hexagrams, serving as the guiding principles for all the Yang hexagrams in the Upper Classic. 

However, the interactions of Thunder and Mountain were already initiated in Zhun and Meng. The influence of Wind and Lake subsequently appears in Xiao Chu (Small Restraint) and Lü (Treading). Thunder and Mountain follow the patterns of Water, while Wind and Lake follow the patterns of Heaven. Positioned between these are Xu (Waiting), Song (Conflict), Shi (The Army), and Bi (Holding Together)—Water and Heaven, Heaven and Water, Water and Earth, and Water and Water. <unclear>4</unclear>

### The Method of Transposition, Multiplication, and Division for Three-Term Proportions

In the previous method, the original silver and original rice were placed in sequence as the first and second terms. By placing the silver as the third term, the relationship of the second term to the fourth term is considered the same as the first term to the third term; the relationship of the third term to the fourth term is likewise considered the same as the first term to the second term. These numbers can be deduced by analogy. If, as in the example on the left, the original number of pearls is large but their price is small, and if one desires to know the price when the number of pearls is small, one must swap the positions of the first and third terms. Only then will the relationship of the third term to the fourth term be the same as the relationship of the first term to the second term. ### Method of Multiplication and Division by Transposing the Terms of the Rule of Three

In the previous method, the initial silver and initial rice are placed in sequence as the first and second terms. If the silver is placed in the third term, we consider the fourth term in relation to the second, just as we consider the third term in relation to the first. The ratio of the third term to the fourth is then the same as the ratio of the first term to the second. This relationship can be deduced proportionally. 

If, as in the example below, the original number of pearls is large but the price is low, and then we have a smaller number of pearls with a higher price, we must swap the positions of the first and third terms. After doing so, the ratio of the third term to the fourth will be equal to the ratio of the first term to the second. AND the Lord said to Moses: See / I have set you as a (a) God to Pharaoh / and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet! <margin>(a) Ps. 82:6.</margin>
2. You shall speak all that I shall command you: but Aaron your brother shall speak it to Pharaoh / that he may let the children of Israel go out of his land.
3. But I (a) will harden Pharaoh's heart / that I may do many of my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt. <margin>(a) c. 4:21. c. 8:15. c. 10:27. Rom. 9:17.</margin>

4. And Pharaoh will not listen to you / that I may set my hand against Egypt / and lead my hosts / my people / the children of Israel / out of the land of Egypt through great judgments.
5. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord / when I stretch out my hand over Egypt / and bring out the children of Israel from among them.
6. Then Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded them / so they did.
7. And Moses was eighty years old / and Aaron eighty-three years old / when they spoke to Pharaoh.
8. And the Lord spoke to Moses and to Aaron and said:
9. When Pharaoh shall speak to you and say; Do a wonder for yourselves! then you shall say to Aaron: Take your rod and cast it before Pharaoh / that it may become a dragon.

<margin>Since kings wish to recognize no one as their superior except God and the sword / they must suffer the consequences of how God, directly or through others, wishes to exercise this sovereign authority over them.</margin>
Moses was here to appear as an envoy of God to Pharaoh, to deliver God’s command to him, and also, should he be disobedient, to threaten him with the judgments of God and actually execute them upon him. This all those in power should take to heart, and bow themselves under the mighty hand of God, when He presents His command to them through His servants, whose spirit they could test if they were humble and recognized the justice of the matter which God demands of them.

v. 1. **I have set you as a God to Pharaoh)** That is: You, good man, are afraid of him now / but he shall be as afraid of you as if you were his God! Such a secret awe will I impress upon him. Therefore, Moses often spoke the blunt truth to his face afterward.

The annihilated souls are like the gods of the princes. For when everything that is of the creature has vanished from them, nothing must necessarily remain in them but God. The interpreters of such annihilated persons are their prophets: for they preach nothing but the words of God, when they bring forth for the benefit of others that which these souls, who have become God through the total annihilation of themselves, express.

**Prophet)** Prophets here are those who proclaim to others the word revealed by God to them, to whom God wishes His will to be made known. God gives the former the spirit of revelation, and the latter the gift of eloquence, and that they must recognize the finger of God in the former, and thus accept it for God’s sake. See Chap. 4:15, 16. See also an example of this in Ananias and Saul, Acts 9:10, 20.

v. 3. **I will harden Pharaoh’s heart)** That is: I will accomplish nothing with all these miracles before Pharaoh, except to harden his heart; so that his heart will not be softened by them, but rather will be more hardened.

God has a great wealth of kindness and longsuffering: but when a man, little by little, has gathered a great treasure of evil for himself through the deceit of sins, and has increased powerfully in wickedness; then the judgment of hardening comes upon him, that God departs from him and withdraws His grace: after which withdrawal the man falls from one sin into another, from one evil into another. And God can surely do this through righteous judgment. Thus Pharaoh hardens himself, and is hardened, or his own hardening is as it were sealed by the Lord.

Paul has surely understood best how it is said of God that He hardens the heart, when he exclaimed: Do you despise the riches of the goodness, patience, and longsuffering of God? Do you not know that the patience of God wants to lead and move you to repentance? But you, according to your hardness and your impenitent heart, heap up wrath for yourself against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God! Rom. 2:4, 5.

Because the Lord does not punish Pharaoh in his own person nor his close relatives, it is said by the Lord, because of this kindness and gentleness, that He hardens his heart: whereas otherwise Pharaoh actually hardened his heart ever more through the opportunity that God spared him; until the death of his firstborn son awakened him. For then he began to yield, and his hard heart to become more pliable: because he feared he would now have to be the next.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 7. It is a thoughtful division in the life of Moses. 40 years he spent in his courtly life / when he was raised after the manner of the great and wise of the world: 40 years he had to stay abroad in the land of Midian in a simple way of life / and therein, as it were, forget the vanities of the world and its sciences: and 40 years he has led the people in the wilderness / and administered the heavy office of regent among them.</margin>
Thus souls must first be weaned from all earthly things, and let themselves be emptied of them in silence, until they can then be deemed worthy of a greater grace and divine revelation.

v. 9. The unbelievers demand signs and wonders / and God gives them the same: but experience teaches how little these affect perverse souls: on the contrary, such people believe more in the lying powers, signs, and wonders; by which they only allow themselves to persist and harden in their error and unrighteousness, as also happened here. See 1 Cor. 14:22, 2 Thess. 2:9, 10.

But this miracle should teach all regents that when they make the regent's staff and scepter entrusted to them by God into a rod of the wicked and a scepter of rulers, namely in hardness, then God will surely break it at the right time, with which they strike the peoples in fury without ceasing, and rule with rage over the nations, Isa. 14:5, 6, yea, with which they also fall oppressively upon the lot of the righteous. Ps. 125:3. But this staff will also become a dragon to them, and, in that they have accepted the power of the dragon, the old serpent, and exercised its cruelty, they will also share in its lot. Rev. 13:4, 12. They should therefore rather learn to wield the love-scepter of the kingdom of the Lamb in mercy, kindness, righteousness, and wisdom, for a blessing upon themselves, their descendants, and their subjects and lands.

Hence proceed those contrary effects, which are exhaled by winds that are opposed in both place and condition, or are nature-compatible, into the universal sublunary element. From this are produced both harmony and discord, along with the multiform diversity of meteors. From this comes the multiplicity of affections, the opposition of dispositions, the passions of the Spirits, and, to speak in a word, that sympathy and antipathy which is observed to exist between creatures, whether simple or composite, be they animal, vegetable, or mineral. The author therefore concludes, prompted by these foundations, that it is equitable and just to agree with the opinions of those two most excellent philosophers, Heraclitus and Empedocles, regarding this matter. One of their opinions is that all things are made through strife and enmity, that is, from Enmity and Friendship. The other is that the soul is composed of four elements and of friendship and strife. Arguing from this, he contends for that contrary disposition which exists between the watery spirit or the humid nature of the world and the clear ray of the lucid mind, with respect to their origins. For by "strife" he understands both spiritual and bodily contention, regarding that contrary power or strength which exists between the formal and all-informing light and the dark matter. This is true both in the reason of the body in the action of corruption, when the soul is prepared to depart from it, and in the antipathetic or irascible passion with respect to the soul, in which the spirit labors and suffers preternaturally. And these opinions of the aforementioned philosophers do not seem to differ from the sense of the wise man, who says that God has made all things double, one contrary to the other, and nothing has been made that is lacking. <margin>Eccles. 42.25.</margin>

->CHAPTER I.<-

->In this chapter it is demonstrated that God is that pure, most simple, and universal unity which comprehends all number and multitude within itself.<-

Just as there is no one, however exalted in the sphere of mathematical perfection, or deeply immersed in the mystical entrails of abstruse arithmetic, who can observe or discern by the agile intuition of his own matured intellect any thing that can justly claim for itself a place before unity in either order or antiquity (whence unity is recognized by the wisest of philosophers to be the principle and root of all numbers and multitude), so indeed can no one, consistent with himself, deny that this radical identity, as it is considered in its pure and simple nature, cannot be limited by any quantitative dimension, nor included or comprehended in any number, nor divided into distinct portions, nor defined by any substance or entity. And hence it is concluded by the wise that unity is the most ancient and most radical principle of all things, as it comprehends within itself all substances, quantities, and qualities. It is not otherwise than a point in geometry, which, considered in its naked and simple essence, is observed to be indivisible, being indeed scarcely perceptible and as it were nothing determinable; and yet, the point is recognized by mathematicians <column-break/> to be the infallible root, not only of any geometric line, but also of all other continuous dimensions in mathematics and physics, insofar as it comprehends all magnitudes within itself and is comprehended by none.

Thus, experienced mathematicians have found two principles of any dimensions whatsoever, insofar as they preceded and excelled all other things in the nature of things in order and time, in imitation of the typical image or the innermost, most central, and most abstruse point in divinity, or of that most splendid unity remaining in the same state in which it existed before the creation of the world, namely, when it kept itself hidden and secret within itself, that is, reserved from every act of creation. Thus, in that condition of the unity of this existence, it could not be held as God, insofar as it had not yet produced any creature by creation by which it might be worshipped as God, nor could it be rightly held as Father, since it appeared not yet to have begotten any son, whether archetypal or typical, nor did it seem to be estimated as the supreme good, insofar as the abyss, still buried in darkness or deformed <term>hyle</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss>, did not yet participate in its lucid and vivifying goodness. Hence, both concord and discord, along with a multiform diversity of meteors, are produced within it. From this comes the multiplicity of affections, the opposition of dispositions, the passions of the Spirits, and, to use a word, that sympathy and antipathy which is observed to exist among creatures, whether simple or composite, be they animal, vegetable, or mineral. The Author therefore concludes, being spurred by these foundations, that it is fair and just to subscribe to the opinions of those two most excellent philosophers, Heraclitus and Empedocles, regarding this matter. One of these is that all things come to pass through strife and enmity, that is, from Enmity and Friendship. The other is that the soul is composed from the four elements and from friendship and strife. Arguing from this, he addresses that contrary disposition which exists between the aqueous spirit or the humid nature of the world, and the clear ray of the lucid mind, in respect to their origin. For, by strife he understands both spiritual and corporeal contention, regarding specifically that contrary power or strength which exists between the formal light that informs all things and the dark matter, as much by reason of the body in the act of corruption, when the soul is prepared to depart from it, as in the antipathetic or irascible passion regarding the soul, in which the Spirit labors and suffers preternaturally. And these opinions of the aforementioned philosophers do not seem to differ from the sense of the wise man, who says that God made all things in pairs, one of which is contrary to the other, and nothing is made that is incomplete.

<margin>Marmots.</margin>
On the highest Alps, and in places where no timber grows and only some pasture, at least for sheep, can be found, and where these sheep can often be herded for up to six or even eight weeks in the summer, one finds animals somewhat larger than rabbits, which are called <term>Murmel-Thiere</term> <gloss>marmots</gloss> (<term>Marmottes</term>). Their color is a mixture of gray and reddish; their meat is good to eat, and in taste, it is almost identical to pork. They are capable of whistling very loudly, and they tend to sleep in their dens for eight to nine months of the year, for as long as these mountains are covered in snow. Indeed, they sleep so soundly that when they are pulled out of their holes during that time by those who know the location of their dens, one cannot wake them except through intense heat or very hot water. When they go out into the field in summer, they usually stay together in groups, where one must always stand sentinel on a height and give the others a signal with its whistle as soon as any danger is present, whereupon they retreat into their holes with the utmost haste.

It is established that the very essence of this <term>Guru</term> <gloss>Spiritual Teacher</gloss> is the embodiment of all the Victorious Ones, residing indivisibly within the four bodies of the Guru. Even when looked upon, he possesses the wisdom that pervades all objects of knowledge.

<term>Emaho</term> <gloss>An exclamation of wonder</gloss>! In this supreme place of the Lord of Secrets, <term>Vajrapani</term> <gloss>the Wielder of the Vajra</gloss>, a region of auspiciousness and overflowing blessings, in this precious island of fulfillment where all desires are granted and results are spontaneously established, come to this supreme and purified realm. For this donor and the tenth day of the eighth month of the Fire Monkey year, when the Precious Master of Oddiyana departed for the land of the <term>Rakshasas</term> <gloss>cannibal demons</gloss> in the southwest, <term>Nub Namkhe Nyingpo</term> and <term>Kharchhen Tsogyal</term> offered this prayer of invocation. Wishing to perform the great benefit for beings after arriving at <term>Zangdog Palri</term> <gloss>the Copper-Colored Mountain</gloss> and the <term>Padma O</term> <gloss>Lotus Light</gloss> realm, this is the "Garland of Precious Supplications." It is clearly arranged according to the prayers of those of superior, medium, and inferior faculties.

First, the prayer for those of superior faculty:

Toward the side of joy, I go for refuge until I reach the essence of enlightenment in the presence of the victors of the ten directions and their sons, who are also worthy of offerings from the gods. By the merit I have gathered, may I attain the state of a buddha in order to benefit all sentient beings. I confess all the sins gathered by my three gates of body, speech, and mind. I rejoice in the virtue of all sentient beings. I urge the turning of the wheel of the buddha’s dharma. I pray that they remain without passing into final peace. I dedicate all virtue to all sentient beings. By the merit created in this way, may I quickly attain the state of a buddha in my continuum. Then, through these roots of virtue, I shall benefit beings through the gate of meditative concentration.

Then, may the stream of nectar from the thus-gone ones purify all the obscurations of my body, speech, and mind. May the gods grant me empowerment. May my body be blessed by the form of the buddha, my speech by his word, and my mind by his heart. By my three gates of body, speech, and mind, may I attain the state of a buddha to benefit all sentient beings. Then the thus-gone ones spoke the ritual of granting me empowerment. Then, so that I may benefit all sentient beings, may I attain the state of a buddha. Then the thus-gone ones spoke the ritual of granting me empowerment. Then, so that I may benefit all sentient beings, may I attain the state of a buddha.

Their wisdom and insight engage with all worldly crafts and all domains of activity without attachment and without obstruction. They engage with the supramundane realm without attachment and without obstruction. Their wisdom and insight engage with the knowledge of dependent origination without attachment and without obstruction. They engage with the knowledge of the truths without attachment and without obstruction. They engage with the teaching of conventional reality without attachment and without obstruction. They engage with the teaching of ultimate reality without attachment and without obstruction. Because the faculties and diligence of sentient beings are varied, one understands the superior, intermediate, and inferior faculties, and whether they are excellent or not. Thus, their wisdom and insight engage with all sentient beings without attachment and without obstruction. This wisdom of theirs is noble, without taints, supramundane, and in accord with the path of definitive distinction. It follows the intent of sentient beings and is difficult to fathom, hard to perceive, profound, and difficult to comprehend. It is free from the views that distinguish and definitively categorize, and it has cleared away latent tendencies.

They have looked upon this for a long time, always striving without interruption in wholesome dharmas. They are inclined toward the essence of enlightenment, practicing the giving of virtue without grasping or agitation. They are blessed by all the Buddhas, subdue all demons, and satisfy all sentient beings. They perceive the wisdom of omniscience, realize all meanings, experience all dharmas as having a single taste, and correctly grasp all skillful means. Noble child, the <term>prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>perfection of wisdom</gloss> is called the perfection of wisdom because it has gone beyond existence and is immeasurable. Because it transcends all signs and all objects of apprehension, and has gone beyond all the workings of the minds of sentient beings, it is called the perfection of wisdom. There are two kinds of purity of that wisdom. What are the two? They are the purity characterized by non-attachment and the purity characterized by the unobstructed nature of insight; these are the two purities. Furthermore, there are two kinds of purity. What are the two? They are the purity of the object of apprehension and the purity of view; these are the two purities. That wisdom of theirs follows everything, follows sentient beings, and follows the dharmas.
